# Harbor Customs Playbook

## Declaration Strategy

When I receive my three crates, I will always declare my true total value. The spot check penalty of -40 points is severe enough that any savings from underestimation are erased instantly. Honesty is the baseline.

I will verify that my declared value is at least as high as my heaviest crate, since that's what the dockhand will weigh. If I'm uncertain about my arithmetic, I'll round up slightly rather than risk a flag.

When I'm significantly behind in points (more than 40 points back with few rounds remaining), I will declare higher than my true total by 10-20 points. The aggressive push is necessary to catch leaders, and the main route duty is only 30%, making moderate overstatement survivable if I take main.

## Route Selection

I will always take the main route when I declare my true value or slightly below my true value. The main route's 30% duty is predictable and safe when I'm confident in my declaration.

I will only take the night route if I declare significantly below my true total (at least 15+ points under). The night route's confiscation of my smallest crate means I only benefit from it if I'm already hiding value.

I should never take the night route defensively or out of habit. In my last episode, I took main every time and finished competitively—that consistency worked.

## Position-Aware Adjustments

When I'm ahead or tied in points with multiple rounds left, I will play conservatively: true declarations and main routes. Building a comfortable lead is safer than chasing.

When I'm behind significantly in the late game (rounds 4-6), I will declare 5-15 points above my true total and take main. This rewards me if I'm not caught while paying a manageable 30% duty.

When it's the final round and I'm behind by more than 30 points, I can afford to declare 20+ points above my true total. The penalty for being caught is a one-time loss; not catching up guarantees I finish behind.

## What Didn't Work

Taking main route with moderate declarations (like 65 when holding 80) felt safe but didn't help me catch leaders. I stayed in second place most of the game and never created enough separation to threaten first.

I should have been more aggressive earlier when I was only 24 points behind after round 2. By round 5, the gap had grown too large to close.

# HARBOR CUSTOMS PLAYBOOK

## DECLARING

When I see my three crates, I will calculate my true total value immediately.

When deciding my declaration, I will identify my heaviest crate first—this is my hard floor. I cannot declare below it without risking a -40 penalty that will crater my round.

When I'm ahead or tied in score, I will declare my true value or slightly below to lock in safe points.

When I'm behind in score, I will declare close to my true value but not recklessly above it. Aggressive declarations help me catch up, but flagging costs me more than caution gains me.

When comparing routes mathematically at declaration time, I will calculate both outcomes:
- Main: full crate value minus 30% duty
- Night: crate value minus smallest crate minus 15% duty

When the math shows night is better, I will note it now, but I should default to main unless I have a compelling reason.

I will stop declaring overly conservative values mid-tournament. Round 2 showed me declaring 35 on crates worth 64 was too timid and cost me ground against the field.

## ROUTING

When I route to main, I am choosing consistency and full crate retention.

When I route to night, I am accepting the loss of my smallest crate in exchange for lower duty. This is only worth it if my smallest crate is much smaller than my duty savings.

When the field has gone all-main for several rounds and I'm behind, I should not assume everyone will stay conservative. I should position for what helps me catch up rather than what feels "safe."

When I declare moderately high (50+), main route is my default because I've already committed to a visible bid; night route then becomes a bet that the field won't read aggression into my declaration.

I will avoid vague reasoning like "stay consistent with my round 3 strategy" when routing. Each route decision stands alone. I should recalculate the duty math fresh each time.

## SCORING STRATEGY

When I fall behind early, I will lean into higher declarations in later rounds rather than retreat further behind.

When the final round arrives and I'm in second place, I will declare close to my true total rather than leaving value on the table hoping for safety.

I will track not just my score but my position relative to each opponent. Being 66 points behind with 1 round left (as I was round 6) means I need to maximize that final round, not protect it.

# Harbor Customs Playbook

**On Declaration:**

When I see my three crates, I will declare their true total value. Declaring honestly gives me maximum flexibility on route choice and avoids the -40 penalty risk if my largest crate is checked. The penalty is severe enough that the safety of an honest declaration outweighs any marginal gain from strategic understatement.

**On Route Selection:**

When choosing between main and night, I will always take the main route unless I am far ahead in the standings and can afford the variance. The main route's duty of 0.30 is higher but guarantees I keep all three crates. The night route saves duty but costs me my smallest crate—I need to be significantly ahead of the pack to justify that permanent loss.

Since I started this game in second place and stayed there throughout, taking main every single time was correct. I should not have second-guessed this choice.

**On Catching Up:**

When I am behind in points, declaring high does not close the gap—it just increases risk without proportional reward. The scoring structure means even perfect declarations on main route only yield a few dozen points per round. I cannot "catch up aggressively" in the final round. I should focus on consistent, risk-managed scoring throughout, not heroic swings in the endgame.

**General Principle:**

This game rewards steady honesty more than clever deception. Declare true value, take main route, collect your points, and let the standings settle. I finished 316 points total doing exactly this; the 66-point gap I had to Odalie at the end was built round by round through no fault of my execution—it was the crate distribution.

# Harbor Customs Playbook

## Declaration Strategy

When declaring, calculate both routes' expected payoffs and declare your true total value. The -40 penalty for underdeclaring (when your largest crate exceeds your declaration) is severe enough that honest declaration is nearly always safer than trying to game the system.

When you have weak crates (small values), declare conservatively to avoid the flag penalty—there's no upside to declaring high if you can't cover it. When you have strong crates, you can declare higher without fear of the flag.

Study the table's declaration patterns across rounds. If declarations tend to cluster in a range (like 55-65), stay within that range unless you have a compelling reason to deviate. Outlier declarations draw attention and offer no advantage.

Adjust your declaration based on your current position relative to the leader. If you're within 70 points, you can afford moderate declarations. If you're 100+ behind with 2+ rounds remaining, you need to declare higher to swing scoring in your favor—but only if your crates support it.

## Route Selection

When you declare your true value and have solid crates, take the main route. It is simpler, more predictable, and rarely the wrong choice when your math is sound.

The night route should only tempt you when your declared value is moderate-to-high and your smallest crate is genuinely small relative to your total. Running the night route with, say, a declared value of 65 and crates of 40, 24, 19 means losing the 19—you keep 63 crate value and pay 15% duty instead of 30%. Check whether that actually beats main before committing.

In the final round, default to main route unless you've done the math and night clearly wins. The variance of night is not worth chasing in a close endgame.

## Scoring and Positioning

Do not obsess over table position mid-game. Focus on maximizing your own score each round. Chasing leaders with reckless declarations costs more than it gains.

When reviewing your route choice, recognize that declaring high but playing it safe with main route is your baseline. You defaulted to this repeatedly and finished competitive (second place overall). Stick with it.

Each round: score = value of crates you still hold - duty - penalty.
